en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 85, the Discourse to Prince Bodhi.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Suṃsumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park.
Now at that time Prince Bodhi had a palace named Kokanada that had recently been built, unoccupied by any ascetic, brahmin, or human being whatsoever.
Then Prince Bodhi addressed the young brahmin Sañjikāputta:

“Come, friend Sañjikāputta, go to where the Blessed One is. Having approached, pay homage with your head at the Blessed One’s feet in my name, and inquire after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical vigor, strength, and well-being, saying:
‘Venerable sir, Prince Bodhi pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and inquires after his freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical vigor, strength, and well-being.
And speak thus:”
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, please accept tomorrow’s meal from Prince Bodhi.
“Very well, sir,” the young brahmin Sañjikāputta replied to Prince Bodhi. He then approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the young brahmin Sañjikāputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Prince Bodhi pays homage with his head at the feet of Master Gotama; he inquires after your health, freedom from illness, physical ease, strength, and well-being.
And he says this:
‘May Master Gotama, together with the community of monks, please accept tomorrow’s meal from Prince Bodhi.’”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the young brahmin Sañjikāputta, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat and approached Prince Bodhi; having approached, he said this to Prince Bodhi:
“We have spoken to the venerable Gotama on your behalf.”
“Prince Bodhi pays homage with his head at the feet of Master Gotama; he inquires after your health, freedom from illness, physical vigor, strength, and well-being.
And he says this:
‘May Master Gotama, together with the community of monks, please accept tomorrow’s meal from Prince Bodhi.’”
"And the ascetic Gotama has consented.
Then, at the end of that night, Prince Bodhi had various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft,
prepared in his own residence, and had the Kokanada palace strewn with white cloth from one end to the other.
Standing on the steps at the rear, he addressed the young brahmin Sañjikāputta:
“Come, dear Sañjikāputta, go to the Blessed One and, having approached him, announce the time, saying:
‘Venerable sir, it is time; the meal is ready.’”
“Yes, sir,” the young brahmin Sañjikāputta replied to Prince Bodhi. He then approached the Blessed One and, having arrived, announced the time to him:
“It is time, Master Gotama; the meal is ready.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of Prince Bodhi.
Now at that time, Prince Bodhi was standing outside the gatehouse, waiting for the Blessed One.
Prince Bodhi saw the Blessed One coming from afar;
having seen him, he went out to meet him, paid homage to the Blessed One, and placing him in front, proceeded toward the Kokanada Palace.
Then the Blessed One stood leaning against the last step of the staircase.
Then Prince Bodhi said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One ascend the cloths, may the Sugata ascend the cloths.”
“...which would lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time.
When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.
A second time also... [as before]...
A third time, Prince Bodhi said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One mount the cloths, Lord; may the Sugata mount the cloths;
may it be for my long-term welfare and happiness.”
Then the Blessed One looked toward the Venerable Ānanda.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda said this to Prince Bodhi:
"Prince, let the cloths be gathered up."
“The Blessed One will not step upon a cloth rug;
the Tathāgata has compassion for future generations.
Then Prince Bodhi, having had the cloths gathered away, prepared seats on the upper terrace of the Kokaṇada palace.
Then the Blessed One, having ascended the Kokanada palace, sat down upon the prepared seat together with the community of bhikkhus.
Then Prince Bodhi, with his own hands, satisfied and served the community of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods.
When the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, Prince Bodhi took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Prince Bodhi said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it occurs to me thus:
‘Happiness is not to be attained through happiness; rather, happiness is to be attained through suffering.’”
“Furthermore, Prince, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully enlightened, this occurred to me:
‘Happiness is not to be attained through happiness; rather, happiness is to be attained through suffering.
Then, Prince, at a later time, while I was still young, with hair still very black and in the prime of my youth, I thought:”

Endowed with the prime of youth, I went forth from the home life into homelessness, shaving off my hair and beard and donning saffron robes, even though my parents were unwilling and wept with tearful faces.
Having thus gone forth, seeking what is wholesome and searching for the unsurpassed, supreme state of peace, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma. Having approached him, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
‘Friend Kālāma, I wish to lead the holy life under this Dhamma and Discipline.
When this was said, Prince, Āḷāra Kālāma said this to me:
‘May the Venerable One dwell here. I am your teacher.’”
"Such is this Dhamma that a wise person, in no long time, might realize for themselves through direct higher knowledge their own teacher’s doctrine, and having attained it, dwell therein.
Prince, I soon mastered that Dhamma quickly.

Prince, at that very stage—with merely the striking of the lips and mere prattle—I claimed to possess the talk of knowledge, and I professed that I knew and saw the talk of the elders, both myself and others.
Then, Prince, it occurred to me:
“Āḷāra Kālāma does not proclaim that he has realized this Dhamma through his own direct higher knowledge and dwells having attained it merely on the basis of faith;
surely Āḷāra Kālāma dwells knowing and seeing this Dhamma.”
Then, Prince, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma and, having approached him, said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
“To what extent, friend Kālāma, do you declare that you have, by realizing it for yourself with direct knowledge, entered upon and abide in this Dhamma?
When this was said, Prince, Āḷāra Kālāma declared the base of nothingness.
Then, Prince, it occurred to me:
‘Āḷāra Kālāma has faith, and I too have faith;
Āḷāra Kālāma has energy, and I too have energy... [and so on].
There is mindfulness … concentration … wisdom; I too have wisdom.
‘What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Āḷāra Kālāma declared he had personally realized through direct knowledge, attained, and dwelt in?
Prince, not long after that, I quickly realized that Dhamma through my own direct knowledge, attained it, and dwelt in it.
Then, Prince, I went to where Āḷāra Kālāma was, and having approached him, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
“Friend Kālāma, is it to this extent that you have realized this Dhamma for yourself through direct higher knowledge, and having attained it, do you proclaim it?
“It is to this extent, friend, that I have realized this Dhamma for myself through direct higher knowledge, and having attained it, I proclaim it.
“Friend, it is to this extent that I too dwell having realized this Dhamma for myself through direct higher knowledge, and having attained it.”
“It is a gain for us, friend, it is a great fortune for us, friend,
that we see such a venerable one as a fellow-celibate. Thus,

that Dhamma which I have realized for myself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered upon it, and proclaim it— that very same Dhamma you dwell having realized for yourself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered upon it.”

The Dhamma that you have realized for yourself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered into it, is the very Dhamma that I have realized for myself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered into it, and I proclaim it.
Thus, the Dhamma that I know, you know that same Dhamma; the Dhamma that you know, I know that same Dhamma.
Thus, as I am, so are you; as you are, so am I.
"Come now, friend, let us both, being tranquil, lead this group.
Thus, Prince, Āḷāra Kālāma, though he was my teacher, placed me—his own pupil—in a position equal to himself and honored me with great honor.
Then, Prince, it occurred to me:
‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, nor to Nibbāna, but only as far as rebirth in the base of nothingness.
Prince, having found that Dhamma unsatisfactory, I became disillusioned with it and left.
Prince, seeking what was wholesome and searching for the supreme state of peace, I approached Uddaka Rāmaputta and, having approached him, said this to Uddaka Rāmaputta:
‘Friend, I wish to lead the holy life under this Dhamma and Discipline.
When this was said, Prince, Udaka Rāmaputta said this to me:
‘May the venerable one dwell here.’”
‘Such is this Dhamma that a wise person, in no long time, having realized for himself through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine, might dwell having attained it.
Prince, I soon and quickly mastered that Dhamma.
Prince, with merely the flapping of my lips and the mere prattle of my tongue, I spoke words of knowledge and claimed, ‘I know and see,’ both myself and others.
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
"Rāma did not proclaim that he had entered upon and dwelt in this Dhamma having realized it for himself through direct higher knowledge merely out of faith;
surely Rāma lived knowing and seeing this Dhamma."
Then, Prince, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta and, having approached him, said this to Udaka Rāmaputta:
"To what extent, friend, did Rāma declare: 'Having realized this Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge, I enter upon and abide in it'?
When this was said, Prince, Udaka Rāmaputta declared the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
‘It was not only Rāma who had faith; I too have faith.
It was not only Rāma who had energy... [and so on].
There is mindfulness… concentration… wisdom; I too have wisdom.
“What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Rāma declared he had personally realized through direct knowledge and dwelt in, having attained it?
Prince, not long after that, I quickly realized that Dhamma through my own direct knowledge and dwelt in its attainment.
Then, Prince, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta and, having approached him, said this to Udaka Rāmaputta:
“Friend, did Rāma declare this Dhamma after having realized it for himself through direct knowledge and attained it, only to this extent?
“Friend, Rāma did indeed declare this Dhamma after having realized it for himself through direct knowledge and attained it to this extent.
“Friend, I too dwell having realized this Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge and attained it to this same extent.”
“It is a gain for us, friend, it is a great fortune for us, friend,
that we see such a venerable one as a fellow-celibate. Thus,
that Dhamma which Rāma himself realized through direct knowledge, attained, and declared, you yourself dwell having realized and attained that very Dhamma through direct knowledge.”

That Dhamma which you have realized for yourself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered into it, Rāma has proclaimed, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered into it.
Thus, that Dhamma which Rāma directly knew, you know that same Dhamma; that Dhamma which you know, Rāma directly knew that same Dhamma.
In this way, as Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma.
"Come now, friend, you yourself lead this group.
Thus, Prince, Udaka Rāmaputta, being my fellow celibate practitioner, placed me in the position of a teacher and honored me with great honor.
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:

‘This teaching does not lead to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to awakening, nor to Nibbāna; it leads only as far as rebirth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Prince, having found that teaching unsatisfactory, I became disillusioned with it and departed.
Prince, seeking what is wholesome and searching for the supreme state of peace, I wandered by stages through Magadha until I arrived at Uruvelā, the village of Senā.

There I saw a delightful stretch of land, a charming woodland grove, and a river flowing with clear water and beautiful landing-stairs; it was a pleasant place, surrounded by a village for alms-gathering.
Then, Prince, this thought occurred to me:

“Truly, this is a delightful stretch of land, a charming woodland grove, and a river flows here with clear water and beautiful landing-stairs; it is a pleasant place, surrounded by a village for alms-gathering.”
"Truly, this is sufficient for a clansman who seeks to strive in order to strive.
Then, Prince, I sat right there, thinking:
"This is sufficient for striving."
Furthermore, prince, three similes occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

Suppose, prince, there were a wet, sappy piece of wood placed in water, and then a man would come along bringing a fire-drill: [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the full simile continues with the man attempting to produce fire by rubbing the fire-drill against the wet wood, which is impossible because the wood is damp.*
‘I shall produce fire; I shall manifest heat.
What do you think, prince, would that man, taking an upper fire-stick and rubbing it against that wet, sap-filled piece of wood placed in the water, succeed in producing fire and manifesting heat?”
“No, venerable sir.
And why is that? Because, venerable sir, that log is wet and full of sap, and moreover it has been placed in water.”
“And furthermore, that man would simply partake in fatigue and vexation.
“In the same way, Prince, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell neither physically nor mentally withdrawn from sensual pleasures,
and whatever sensual desire, sensual affection, or sensual infatuation they have toward those pleasures— ”
The thirst for sensual pleasures and the fever of sensual pleasures have not been well-abandoned within them, nor have they been well-calmed.

Whether those venerable ascetics and brahmins experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted means, they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed enlightenment;

and even if those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not experience such painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted means, they are still incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed enlightenment.
"Prince, this first simile occurred to me, which is marvelous and unprecedented, never heard before.
Furthermore, Prince, a second simile occurred to me, which is marvelous and unprecedented, never heard before.
It is just as if, Prince, there were a piece of wet, sap-filled wood placed far from water on dry land."
Then, suppose a man were to come along carrying an upper fire-stick, thinking:
‘I shall produce fire; I shall manifest heat.
What do you think, prince?
“Would that man, taking a wet, sap-filled piece of wood and placing it far from water on dry land, produce fire and manifest heat by using an upper fire-stick and rubbing it?
“Certainly not, venerable sir. And why is that?”
“For just as, venerable sir, even though a piece of wet, sap-filled wood were placed far away from water on dry land,
that person would nevertheless partake of exhaustion and distress—
just so, prince, those ascetics or brahmins who, both in body and in mind...”

They dwell withdrawn from sensual pleasures; yet whatever sensual desire, sensual affection, sensual infatuation, sensual thirst, sensual fever they have toward those pleasures has not been well-abandoned within them, nor is it well-pacified.

Even if these venerable recluses and brahmins experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted means, they are still incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

"Those venerable recluses and brahmins, Prince, who undergo self-inflicted painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, have not attained them; they are indeed incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
This, Prince, was the second simile that occurred to me—extraordinary and unheard of before.
Furthermore, Prince, a third simile occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before."
"Just as if, prince, there were a dry piece of wood, withered and hollow, lying far from water on dry land.
Then a man might come along carrying an upper fire-stick, thinking:
'I shall produce fire; I shall manifest heat.'"
“What do you think, prince?
Would that man, taking an upper fire-stick and rubbing it against a dry piece of wood—a withered stump set far from water on dry land—be able to produce fire and manifest heat?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“For what reason?
Because that wood, venerable sir, is dry, withered, and shriveled, and moreover it has been placed far away from water on dry land.
“In the same way, prince, whatever ascetics or brahmins, both by body and by mind...”

They dwell withdrawn from sensual pleasures; whatever sensual desire, sensual affection, sensual infatuation, sensual thirst, sensual fever, and sensual passion they have toward sensual pleasures has been well abandoned within them and well stilled.

Even if those venerable recluses and brahmins experience painful, racking, piercing, and bitter feelings resulting from self-inflicted mortification, they are still capable of knowledge, vision, and supreme enlightenment.

"Those venerable recluses and brahmins, O prince, who undergo self-inflicted painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, are indeed capable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
This, O prince, was the third simile that occurred to me—extraordinary and never heard before.
These, O prince, were the three similes that occurred to me, extraordinary and never heard before."
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
“What if I, having clenched my teeth and pressed my tongue against the palate, were to restrain, suppress, and torment the mind with the mind?
So, Prince, having clenched my teeth and pressed my tongue against the palate, I restrained, suppressed, and tormented the mind with the mind.
“Then, prince, as I pressed my teeth against my teeth, pressed my tongue against my palate, and with my mind restrained, suppressed, and tormented the mind, sweat poured from my armpits.
Prince, it was just as if a strong man were to seize a weaker man by the head or by the shoulders and restrain him, suppress him, and torment him.”
In the same way, Prince, when I clenched my teeth, pressed my tongue against the palate, and with my mind restrained, suppressed, and tormented the mind, sweat poured from my armpits.
Yet, Prince, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused;
however, my body was agitated and not calmed because I was so overcome by that painful striving.
Then, Prince, it occurred to me:
"What if I were to practice the meditation of breathlessness?
So, Prince, I suppressed both the inhalation and exhalation through my mouth and nose.
“Prince, when the inhalation and exhalation were stilled at my mouth and nose, there was an intense sound of winds escaping through my ear canals.
Just as there would be an intense sound from a blacksmith’s bellows being blown,
even so, Prince, when the inhalation and exhalation were stilled at my mouth and nose, there was an intense sound of winds escaping through my ear canals.”
"But, prince, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused;
yet my body was restless and unpacified because I was so intent upon that painful exertion.
Then, prince, this thought occurred to me:"
‘What if I were to meditate on the breathless meditation?
Prince, I then suppressed the inhalations and exhalations through my mouth, nose, and ears.
When the inhalations and exhalations were thus suppressed through my mouth, nose, and ears, Prince, violent winds struck my head.
"Just as if, prince, a strong man were to strike one on the head with a sharp spear, even so, prince,
when the inhalations and exhalations were obstructed at my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds churned in my head. Yet, prince,
my energy was aroused and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and undeluded."
Moreover, my body was agitated and uncalmed because of that very painful striving, as I was struck down by the exertion.
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
"What if I were to practice a meditation involving self-starvation?"
So, prince, I stopped the inhalation and exhalation through my mouth, nose, and ears.
When the inhalation and exhalation were stopped through my mouth, nose, and ears, prince, there was an extreme pain in my head.
It was as if, prince, a strong man were to bind a tight leather strap around my head.
In the same way, Prince, when the inhalations and exhalations were obstructed at my mouth, nose, and ears, there was an intense pain in my head.
Yet, Prince, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused;
however, my body was agitated and not calmed because I was so overcome by that painful striving.
Then, Prince, it occurred to me:
“Suppose I were to practice the meditation of breathlessness.
So, Prince, I stopped the inhalation and exhalation through my mouth, nose, and ears.
“Prince, when the inhalations and exhalations were stilled at my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds cut through my belly. Prince,
just as a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice might cut through a cow’s belly with a sharp carving knife, even so, prince,
when the inhalations and exhalations were stilled at my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds cut through my belly.”
"But, prince, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused;
yet my body was agitated and not calmed because of that very painful striving. As I was thus afflicted by the exertion of striving, prince, this thought occurred to me:"
‘What if I were to meditate on the breathless meditation?
Prince, I then suppressed the inhalations and exhalations through my mouth, nose, and ears.
When the inhalations and exhalations were thus suppressed through my mouth, nose, and ears, Prince, an intense burning arose in my body.
"Just as if, prince, two strong men were to seize a weaker man by his arms and roast him over a pit of glowing embers, scorching him thoroughly;
even so, prince, when the inhalations and exhalations through my mouth, nose, and ears were obstructed, there was an intense burning in my body.
Yet, prince, my energy remained aroused and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and undeluded."
Moreover, my body was agitated and uncalmed, being struck by that very exertion while I was striving with such painful effort.
And when the deities saw me, Prince, they said:
"The ascetic Gotama has passed away."
Some deities said:
"The ascetic Gotama has not passed away; rather, he is passing away.
Some other deities said:
“The ascetic Gotama has not died, nor is he dying. The ascetic Gotama is an arahant. Such is the dwelling of an arahant.
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
“What if I were to practice the total cutting off of food?”
Then, Prince, deities approached me and said this:
“Do not, dear sir, practice the total cutting off of food.
If you, dear sir, should practice the total cutting off of food, we would infuse divine nutritive essence into your pores, and by that you would subsist.”
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
“If I were to claim to be entirely free from deceit, yet these deities were to infuse divine nutritive essence into my pores and I were to subsist on that, it would be a falsehood for me.
Thus, Prince, I rejected those deities, saying, “Enough!”
Then, Prince, it occurred to me:
“What if I were to take food little by little, even just a handful at a time—whether it be mung bean soup, or lentil soup, or pea soup, or vetch soup?
And so, Prince, I took food little by little, even just a handful at a time—whether it be mung bean soup, or lentil soup, or pea soup, or vetch soup.
As I ate food little by little— whether it was bean soup,
lentil soup, pea soup, or vetch soup— my body reached an extreme degree of emaciation.
Just as the joints of an old cart are held together with straps, so my limbs were held together by skin and sinews due to that very lack of food.
Just as an otter’s foot, so too did my buttocks become like that because of that very scantiness of food.
Just as a string of beads, so too did my spine appear with its vertebrae protruding one after another because of that very scantiness of food.
Just as the rafters of an old shed become sagging and decayed, so too did my ribs become sagging and decayed because of that very scantiness of food.

Just as in a deep well the reflections of the stars at the bottom appear as deep-set depressions, even so in my eye-sockets the pupils appeared as deep-set depressions because of that very lack of food.
Just as a bitter gourd, freshly cut, becomes withered and shriveled by the wind and sun, even so my scalp became withered and shriveled because of that very lack of food.
Thus, Prince, thinking, "I will touch the skin of my belly," I would grasp only my backbone;
and thinking, "I will touch my backbone," I would grasp only the skin of my belly. To such an extent, Prince, did the skin of my belly cling to my backbone because of that scantiness of food.
Thus, Prince, when I thought, "I shall defecate or urinate," I would fall right there face down because of that very meagreness of food.
And so, Prince, seeking to comfort this body, I would rub my limbs with my hand.
As I rubbed my limbs with my hand, Prince, the hairs fell from my body by their very roots because of that very meagreness of food.
Furthermore, Prince, when people saw me, some said: “The ascetic Gotama is dark-complexioned. Some people said: “The ascetic Gotama is not dark-complexioned;
he is olive-skinned. Some people said: “The ascetic Gotama is neither dark-complexioned nor olive-skinned; he has golden skin.”
"As long as my complexion remained so pure and bright, O prince, it was because of that very lack of food; yet it became marred by that same lack of food.
Then, O prince, this thought occurred to me:
'Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past experienced painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted mortification, this is the utmost limit, nothing beyond this.'"

Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted mortification, this is the utmost limit; there is nothing beyond this.
Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present experience painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted mortification, this is the utmost limit;
there is nothing beyond this. Yet, by means of this bitter practice of self-mortification, I do not attain any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
‘Could there perhaps be another path to awakening?
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
‘I recall that while sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree during my father Suddhodana’s work, I was secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states.’”

“Having secluded oneself from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states, having entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion—
could this indeed be the path to enlightenment?”
“Then, prince, my consciousness followed after the memory [of past lives], and the thought occurred to me:
‘This indeed is the path to enlightenment.
Then, prince, this further thought occurred to me:”
‘Why indeed should I fear that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states?
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
‘I do not fear that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.’”
Then, Prince, it occurred to me:
“It is not easy to attain that bliss with a body so excessively emaciated. What if I were to take substantial food, such as boiled rice and sour gruel?
And so, Prince, I took substantial food, boiled rice and sour gruel.
At that time, Prince, the group of five monks were waiting for me with the thought:
“Whatever Dhamma the ascetic Gotama attains, he will declare it to us.
But when I, Prince, took solid food—rice and porridge—then those five monks, having lost faith, departed from me.
“The ascetic Gotama is a glutton, he has abandoned his striving and turned back to luxury.
Then, Prince, having taken solid food and regained strength, secluded from sensual pleasures... [I] entered and dwelt in the first jhāna.
With the stilling of directed thought and evaluation... [I] entered and dwelt in the second jhāna.
I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna… and the fourth jhāna.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
Thus I recollect my manifold past lives, that is to say, one birth, two births... [as far as] thus with their aspects and particulars I recollect my manifold past lives.
This, Prince, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night;
ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose—as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I saw beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and I understood how beings fare according to their kamma... [and so forth].

This, Prince, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night: ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose—just as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
Thus I directly knew, as it really is: "This is suffering" ... pe ... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering";
I directly knew, as it really is: "These are the taints" ... pe ... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints.
As I knew thus and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, my mind was liberated from the taint of existence, and my mind was liberated from the taint of ignorance.
When I was liberated, the knowledge arose: "It is liberated.
I directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This, Prince, was my third [knowledge] in the last watch of the night.
“Knowledge has been attained, ignorance has been dispelled, knowledge has arisen; darkness has been dispelled, light has arisen—just as it happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
‘This Dhamma that I have attained is profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.’”
But this generation delights in attachment, is devoted to attachment, and rejoices in attachment.
For a generation that delights in attachment, is devoted to attachment, and rejoices in attachment, this point is difficult to see: namely, specific conditionality and dependent origination.
This point, too, is difficult to see: namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
‘If I were to teach the Dhamma, and others did not understand me, that would be weariness to me, that would be vexation to me.
And then, Prince, these marvelous verses, never heard before, occurred to me:
‘With difficulty have I attained it;’
Enough now with further exposition;
this Dhamma is not easily awakened to by those who are overcome by lust and hatred.
Those who are stained by passion will not see that which goes against the stream, which is subtle, profound, difficult to perceive, and minute.
"Enveloped by the mass of darkness.
Thus, Prince, as I reflected, my mind inclined toward inaction rather than to teaching the Dhamma.
Then, Prince, the Brahmā Sahampati, knowing with his own mind the reflection in my mind, thought this:

“Alas, sirs, the world is perishing! Alas, sirs, the world is being destroyed! For the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, inclines his mind toward inaction rather than toward teaching the Dhamma.
Then, Prince, Brahmā Sahampati—just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—disappeared from the Brahma-world and reappeared before me.
Then, Prince, Brahmā Sahampati arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward me in salutation, and said this to me:
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma! Let the Sugata teach the Dhamma!
There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma.”
‘There will be those who understand the Dhamma.
This, Prince, is what Brahmā Sahampati said;
having said this, he further spoke as follows:
“In the past, an impure Dhamma appeared among the Magadhans, conceived by those still stained with defilements.
Open this door to the Deathless!”
Listen to the Dhamma awakened to by the Stainless One.
Just as one standing on the summit of a rocky mountain might see the people all around, so too does he look upon the world.
Having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, which is like that, O wise one,
with eyes seeing all around,
you, free from sorrow, look upon the people overwhelmed by sorrow.
Behold those overcome by birth and old age;
arise, O Hero, victor in battle!
O Caravan-leader, free from debt, wander through the world.
"May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma;
there will be those who understand.
Then, Prince, having understood Brahmā’s entreaty and out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha.
“Furthermore, prince, while surveying the world with the eye of a Buddha, I saw beings with little dust on their eyes and those with much dust on their eyes;
those with keen faculties and those with dull faculties; those of good disposition and those of bad disposition; those easy to instruct and those difficult to instruct;
and some who dwell perceiving fear in the blame of the next world, and others who dwell not perceiving fear in the blame of the next world.”
Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, or pink lotuses, or white lotuses, some blue lotuses, pink lotuses,
or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, do not emerge from the water,
and thrive submerged within it; and some blue lotuses, pink lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water...
Some blue lotuses, pink lotuses, or white lotuses born in the water and grown in the water stand level with the surface of the water;
others, born in the water and grown in the water, have risen above the water and stand unsullied by it.
In the same way, Prince, as I surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes.

"O Great King, there are those with great defilements and those with keen faculties, those with dull faculties, those of good disposition and those of bad disposition, those easy to instruct and those difficult to instruct;
some dwell perceiving the fear of blame regarding the world beyond, while others dwell not perceiving the fear of blame regarding the world beyond.
Then, Prince, I replied to Brahmā Sahampati with a verse:"
‘The doors to the Deathless are opened for them;
let those who have ears release their faith.
Perceiving harm [in it], I did not speak what is skillful.’
“O Brahmā, the sublime Dhamma among men!

Then, Prince, Brahmā Sahampati, thinking, “I have been granted permission by the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma,” paid homage to me, circumambulated me with his right side toward me, and vanished right there.
Then, Prince, this thought occurred to me:
‘To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dhamma?
Who will understand this Dhamma quickly?
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
‘This Āḷāra Kālāma is wise, competent, and intelligent; for a long time he has been one whose nature is free from much defilement.
Suppose I were to teach this Dhamma first to Āḷāra Kālāma;
he would quickly understand this Dhamma.’
Then, Prince, a deity approached me and said this:
‘Venerable sir, Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago.
And knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘Āḷāra Kālāma has been dead for seven days.
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
‘Āḷāra Kālāma was indeed a man of great learning.’”
‘If he were to hear this Dhamma, he would quickly understand it.
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
‘To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dhamma?’”
‘Who will quickly understand this Dhamma?
Then, Prince, it occurred to me:
‘This Udaka Rāmaputta is wise, competent, and intelligent; for a long time he has been one whose vision is free from dust.’”
‘What if I were to teach the Dhamma first to Uddaka Rāmaputta?
He would quickly understand this Dhamma.
Then, Prince, a deity approached me and said this:
“Venerable sir, Udaka Rāmaputta died last night.
And the knowledge and vision arose in me:
“Udaka Rāmaputta died last night.”
Then, prince, it occurred to me:
"Uddaka Rāmaputta is indeed a great man of learning.
If he were to hear this Dhamma, he would quickly understand it."
Then, prince, this occurred to me:
“To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?
Who will understand this Dhamma most quickly?”
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
“The group-of-five monks have been very helpful to me, for they attended upon me when I was intent on striving.
What if I were to teach the Dhamma first to the group-of-five monks?”
Then, Prince, this occurred to me:
"Where are the group-of-five monks living now?
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I saw, Prince, the group-of-five monks living at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, Prince, having dwelt at Uruvelā for as long as I pleased, I set out on a wandering tour toward Bārāṇasī.
Along the road between Gayā and the Bodhi tree, Prince, the Ājīvaka Upaka saw me traveling on the highway.
Having seen me, he said this to me:
“Friend, your faculties are serene; the color of your skin is pure and bright.
Under whom, friend, have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess?
When this was said, Prince, I addressed the Ājīvaka Upaka with these verses:
“I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all;
I am unsullied by any phenomena.
Having abandoned everything, I am liberated through the destruction of craving.”
Having realized it for myself, whom should I point to? I have no teacher,
and my equal is not found.
In this world with its devas,
there is no one who is my equal.
For I am the Arhat in the world.
I am the unsurpassed Teacher;
I alone am the Perfectly Enlightened One,
cooled and attained to Nibbāna.
I shall go to the city of Kāsi to set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,
in this world that has become blind.
‘I shall beat the drum of the Deathless.
‘Friend, as you claim for yourself, you are indeed an Arahant, a Conqueror of the Infinite.
‘The Conquerors are indeed like me.’
“Those who have attained the destruction of the taints,
by whom evil states have been conquered—
therefore, Upaka, I am a Conqueror.”
When this was said, Prince, Upaka the Ājīvaka replied, “Perhaps so, friend,” and shaking his head and taking a bypath, he departed.
Then, Prince, wandering by stages on my journey, I approached Bārāṇasī, the Deer Park at Isipatana, where the group of five monks were staying.
The group of five monks saw me coming from afar, Prince.
Having seen him, they settled among themselves:
“Friends, this ascetic Gotama is coming—luxurious, fallen away from his striving, and returned to luxury.
He is not to be saluted, nor is he to be stood up for, nor is his bowl and robe to be received.”
"Moreover, a seat should be set out, thinking: 'If he so desires, he will sit down.
Prince, in whatever manner I approached the group of five monks, in that same manner the group of five monks was unable to maintain their prior agreement.
Some came forward to meet me and received my bowl and robes; some prepared a seat; some set out water for washing the feet.
"Moreover, they address me by name and with the term 'friend.
When this was said, Rājakumāra, I said to the group of five monks:
'Monks, do not address the Tathāgata by name and with the term "friend";'"
“Monks, the Tathāgata is an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Give ear, monks; I shall instruct you in that which has been attained—the Deathless—and I shall teach you the Dhamma.
Practicing in accordance with my instruction, before long, for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness...”
‘Go forth into homelessness; having realized for yourselves through direct knowledge, you shall abide in that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life, even in this very life.
When this was said, Prince, the bhikkhus of the group of five said this to me:
"Even by that conduct, friend Gotama, by that practice, and by those ascetic penances, you did not attain any superhuman state,

any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. How then, now that you are luxurious, have abandoned your striving, and have turned back to luxury, will you attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?"
When this was said, Prince, I said this to the group of five bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is not one who indulges in abundance, nor has he lapsed from his striving, nor has he turned back to abundance.
Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.”
"Listen, bhikkhus! I instruct you in that which has been attained—the Deathless; I teach the Dhamma.

Practicing in accordance with my instruction, before long you yourselves will, in this very life, realize for yourselves the supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which sons of noble family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness."
‘...having realized the higher knowledges for yourselves, you shall dwell having attained them.
A second time, Prince, the group of five monks said this to me:
‘Friend Gotama, by that conduct, by that practice, and by that performance of austerities, you did not even attain [superhuman states].’”
"Superhuman states, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones— how then, since you are now one who indulges in abundance,
has abandoned striving, and has turned back to abundance, will you attain superhuman states, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?
A second time, Prince, I said this to the group of five monks:
“Monks, the Tathāgata is not one who indulges in abundance, nor is he one who has strayed from his exertion, nor has he turned back toward abundance.
Monks, the Tathāgata is an Arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Give ear, monks! The Deathless has been attained; I instruct you, I teach you the Dhamma.”

"Practicing in accordance with what has been instructed, before long you will, by realizing it for yourselves through direct knowledge, enter and dwell in that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, even in this very life."
A third time, Prince, the group of five monks said this to me:

“Friend Gotama, even by that conduct, by that practice, and by that performance of austerities, you did not attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; so why now are you one who indulges in abundance?”
‘Having fallen away from striving, you have turned back toward abundance; will you attain any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?
When this was said, Prince, I said to the group of five monks:
‘Do you recognize, monks, that I have ever before manifested such a thing as this?’”
‘No indeed, Bhante.
‘Monks, the Tathāgata is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One.
Give ear, monks; I shall instruct you in what has been attained—the Deathless; I shall teach you the Dhamma.’
"Practicing in accordance with what has been instructed, before long you will,

by realizing it for yourselves through direct knowledge, enter and dwell in that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, even in this very life."
I was indeed able, Prince, to persuade the group of five monks.
However, Prince, I would instruct two monks while three monks went for alms.
Whatever those three monks brought back from their almsround, with that we six would sustain ourselves.
"Prince, I would give instruction to those three monks as well; two monks would go for alms.
With what the two monks brought back from their alms-round, the group-of-six monks and I would subsist.
Then, Prince, while the monks of the group-of-five were being thus instructed and exhorted by me..."

“Before long, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, they dwelt having attained it.
When this was said, Prince Bodhi addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Venerable sir, how long does it take for a bhikkhu, having obtained the Tathāgata as his leader,

to realize for himself through direct knowledge in this very life, and to enter and dwell in, that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness?”
“In that case, prince, I shall question you about this very matter. Answer it as you see fit.
What do you think, prince:
are you skilled in the art of riding an elephant and wielding the goad?”
“In this way, venerable sir, I am skilled in the art of managing elephants with the goad.
“What do you think, prince?
Suppose a man were to come here saying:”
‘Prince Bodhi knows the art of riding elephants while wielding a goad;
I shall learn that art of riding elephants while wielding a goad in his presence.
Yet he is without faith.
He might not attain whatever can be attained by one endowed with faith.
Furthermore, he might be subject to much illness;
he might not attain whatever can be attained by one who is free from illness.
He would be deceitful and fraudulent;
he would not attain what can be attained by one who is honest and free from fraud.
He would be indolent.
Whatever can be attained by one who has aroused energy, he would not attain it.
And he would be lacking in wisdom;
whatever can be attained by one possessed of wisdom, he would not attain it.
“What do you think, prince, would that man learn from you the craft of handling the elephant-hook with his hands?

“Venerable sir, even if that man possessed only one of those five qualities, he would not learn from me the craft of handling the elephant-hook with his hands; what need is there to mention all five?”
“What do you think, prince?
Suppose a man were to come here and say:
‘Prince Bodhi knows the craft of riding an elephant while holding a goad.’”
‘In his presence I shall learn the craft of riding an elephant and wielding a goad.
He would have faith;
he would attain whatever can be attained by one who has faith.
He would be free from illness;
he would attain whatever can be attained by one who is free from illness.
He would be honest and not deceitful.
He would attain whatever can be attained by one who is honest and free from deceit.
He would also be one whose energy is aroused;
he would attain whatever can be attained by one whose energy is aroused.
He would be wise; he would attain whatever can be attained by one who is wise.
What do you think, prince?
“Would that man, then, learn from you the craft of wielding a goad while mounted on an elephant?

“Venerable sir, even if he possessed only one of these qualities, that man would learn from me the craft of wielding a goad while mounted on an elephant; what need is there to mention one who possesses all five?
“In the same way, prince, there are these five factors of striving.”
What are the five?
Here, prince, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith; he has faith in the awakening of the Tathāgata:

“Thus indeed is that Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.”
He is free from illness and free from affliction, possessing a digestive capacity that is well-balanced—neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and fit for exertion.
He is not fraudulent and not deceitful, revealing himself as he truly is to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life.

He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in his effort, and does not relinquish his burden regarding wholesome states.
He is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
These, Prince, are the five factors of striving.
Possessed of these five factors of striving, Prince, a bhikkhu who has obtained the Tathāgata as his guide—

For seven years, Prince, he might dwell having realized for himself through direct knowledge and attained in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Let alone seven years, Prince;
a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors of striving, obtaining the Tathāgata as his guide—

Having himself realized through direct knowledge and attained in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness,
he might dwell having entered upon it after six years… five years… four years… [or three, two, or one year].
For three years… for two years… for one year.
"Let alone one year, prince.
A bhikkhu endowed with these five factors for striving, having obtained the Tathāgata as his guide, might—

having realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness— abide in its attainment within seven months."
"Let alone seven months, Prince.
A bhikkhu endowed with these five factors of striving, obtaining the Tathāgata as his guide—
that unsurpassed goal for which sons of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness— "
Having realized for oneself through direct knowledge the culmination of the holy life in this very life, one might dwell having attained it for six months… five months… four months…
For three months … for two months … for one month …
Half a month.
Let alone half a month, prince,
a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors for striving, obtaining the Tathāgata as his guide—

“May he dwell for seven days and nights having himself realized through direct knowledge, attained, and entered upon that very goal for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness— that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life, right here and now in this very world.
“Let alone seven days and nights, Prince, O Prince.”
A bhikkhu endowed with these five factors of striving, having obtained the Tathāgata as his guide,

might— having personally realized through direct knowledge and attained in this very life that supreme goal for which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness— dwell having reached the consummation of the holy life within six days and nights...
five days and nights … four days and nights … three days and nights …
Two days and nights...
one day and night.
Let alone one day and night, Prince.

“A bhikkhu endowed with these five factors of striving, if he receives instruction from the Tathāgata, the Guide, will attain distinction in the evening if instructed in the morning, and will attain distinction in the morning if instructed in the evening.
When this was said, Prince Bodhi addressed the Blessed One:
“Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma!”
"For indeed, one instructed in the evening might attain distinction by the morning, and one instructed in the morning might attain distinction by the evening.
When this was said, the young brahmin Sañjikāputta spoke thus to Prince Bodhi:
"In this very way, Master Bodhi..."
‘Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma!’—yet he does not go for refuge to Master Gotama, nor to the Dhamma, nor to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

“Do not say so, friend Sañjikāputta; do not say so, friend Sañjikāputta. Do not misrepresent Master Gotama with such words; it is not good to misrepresent him. Master Gotama would never speak in such a way. Friend Sañjikāputta, Master Gotama has indeed said: ‘Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma! And yet he does not go for refuge to Master Gotama, nor to the Dhamma, nor to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
“I heard this from the noble lady in her presence, friend Sañjikāputta; I received it directly from her.
“On one occasion, friend Sañjikāputta, the Blessed One was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.

Then my noble lady, being pregnant, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side. As she was sitting there, my noble lady said this to the Blessed One:”
“Venerable sir, this boy or girl who has come into my womb goes for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept him as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth as long as life lasts.
“On one occasion, friend Sañjikāputta, the Blessed One was staying right here among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park.”

Then my nurse, carrying me on her hip, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she stood to one side. Standing to one side, my nurse said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this Prince Bodhi goes for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept him as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”
"Friend Sañjikāputta, for a third time I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
The Bodhirājakumāra Sutta is finished; it is the fifth.
